title: The Death Penalty
lead: The law of Moses names death for murder and for a range of religious and sexual crimes. Jews and Christians have long debated how such laws were applied, and whether they say anything about the state's power today.

sections.h: The death penalty across the Bible
sections.b: Genesis 9:6 grounds the penalty for murder in the image of God. The Torah adds death for striking or cursing parents, kidnapping, sorcery, Sabbath breaking, blasphemy, idolatry, adultery, incest, male–male intercourse and bestiality (Exodus 21:12–17; Exodus 31:14; Leviticus 20; Leviticus 24:16–17; Deuteronomy 13; Deuteronomy 22:22). Two or three witnesses are required (Deuteronomy 17:6). The Bible also shows mercy in place of death: God spares Cain (Genesis 4:15) and David (2 Samuel 12:13). The rabbis set strict rules of evidence and debated whether a court should ever execute (Mishnah Makkot 1:10), though they also allowed emergency punishments (Talmud, Sanhedrin 46a). Jesus stops a stoning (John 8:2–11, a passage absent from the earliest manuscripts), while Paul says the state "does not carry the sword for no reason" (Romans 13:4). Christians remain divided on whether the state may still take life.
